clue.text: No doubt she takes people in.

definitions.text: No doubt she takes people in.

parts.words: No doubt she takes people in
parts.note: reads like a swindler who deceives people, but means a woman who receives guests into her home

explanation.surface: A con artist is assumed to be duping her victims.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman entertaining guests welcomes visitors into her house, so she literally takes people in.

annotationWithheld.clue: Quite ordinary behaviour at a normal

clue.text: It's kept in reserve-a kind of heap!

parts.note: stock means kind or breed, as in 'of good stock'
a pile is a heap

explanation.surface: A store set aside is likened to a sort of mound.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard of supplies accumulated for future use is held back as a reserve.

clue.text: Tiresome effect of some common or nuisance.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Tiresome effect of some common or nuisance.', has no hidden run of the five letters: the words cannot supply an E before NNUI, so the text is garbled.

clue.text: Get ready to be taken for a ride?

definitions.text: Get ready to be taken for a ride?

parts.words: Get ready to be taken for a ride
parts.note: sounds like bracing to be cheated, but literally means preparing a horse so someone can ride it

explanation.surface: Someone braces themselves to be swindled.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on a horse's seat and girth is to prepare the animal for a rider.

clue.text: They involve quite a bit of struggling

definitions.text: They involve quite a bit of struggling

parts.words: They involve quite a bit of struggling
parts.note: a plain description of scuffles or brief fights, which consist of grappling

explanation.surface: Some activities demand considerable effort and wrestling.
explanation.definitionFit: Scuffles and wrestling bouts are fights in which people grapple with each other.

clue.text: We are two lions litter'd in one day, And I the elder and more ——" (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: We are two lions litter'd in one day, And I the elder and more

parts.words: We are two lions litter'd in one day, And I the elder and more
parts.note: Caesar's boast in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, where the missing last word of the line is the word wanted

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Caesar compares himself with Danger as twin lions, himself the elder.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Julius Caesar, Act 2 Scene 2, ends the line 'And I the elder and more terrible'.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar claims to be more fearsome and dreadful than Danger itself, completing the quoted line.

clue.text: We are two lions litter'd in one the elder and more no 6, In which to see different grades get quite nonplussed:

indicators.note: different asks for the letters of grades get to be made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Seeing the varied marks awarded leaves someone utterly bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words as held, up to 'In which', are spill-over from the quotation clue above. 'different' makes STAGGERED from GRADES GET.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonished and thrown into confusion, as someone utterly perplexed is.

clue.text: Hopelessly drunk-no head for Bingo!/

indicators.note: no head means the word for very drunk loses its first letter

parts.note: blotto is slang for very drunk

explanation.surface: Someone too inebriated to call out the numbers at a bingo hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance with numbered cards, essentially the same as bingo.

clue.text: Like a double bass taken as one!

definitions.text: Like a double bass taken as one!

parts.words: Like a double bass taken as one
parts.note: a double bass is a string instrument, so it is literally full of strings; the word also means tough and fibrous

explanation.surface: Describing an instrument, or someone treated as a big ungainly fiddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A double bass has strings, so it is string-like, and the word also means fibrous or wiry.

clue.text: Taking off, it's just dejected!

parts.note: add the word 'off' to the wanted word and the phrase means fed up or dejected

explanation.surface: A plane departing, or someone deflated by leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned off' is British slang for fed up or depressed; with 'off' taken on, the word means dejected.
explanation.definitionFit: Toasted or cooked until darker in colour; with 'off' added it becomes a phrase for being fed up.

clue.text: The sort of day by which one might

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'The sort of day by which one might (7)', is cut short after 'might': the defining end of the clue for a very hot day is missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: The sort of day by which one might

clue.text: Hardly the way to stand up medicine ?

definitions.text: Hardly the way to stand up medicine ?

parts.words: Hardly the way to stand up medicine
parts.note: accepting something meekly is the opposite of standing up for yourself, while swallowing a medicine in bed is a literal reading

explanation.surface: Someone is told this is no way to resist, or perhaps to swallow a dose.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept an insult or setback passively, without protest or resistance; also, literally, swallowing a dose while recumbent.

clue.text: It could be raised, said Kipling. East of Suez.

definitions.text: It could be raised, said Kipling. East of Suez.

parts.words: It could be raised, said Kipling. East of Suez
parts.note: Kipling's poem Mandalay speaks of a place east of Suez where a man can raise a craving for drink

explanation.surface: A literary allusion to Kipling's soldier longing for the East.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Mandalay: 'Ship me somewheres east of Suez ... Where there aren't no Ten Commandments an' a man can raise a thirst'.
explanation.definitionFit: A craving for drink, which Kipling's soldier says a man can work up in the East.

clue.text: Kind of pantry, not, it seems, fully stored.

explanation.surface: A larder that is apparently only half full.
explanation.definitionFit: A storeroom in a large house for preserves and drinks; read as two words, space remaining because it is not yet full.

clue.text: A somewhat red-faced way in appear.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'A somewhat red-faced way in appear. (8)', is garbled between 'in' and 'appear': words are missing, so the definition cannot be fixed.
annotationWithheld.clue: A somewhat red-faced way in appear.

clue.text: A mark I make is just toothy.

parts.note: a dent is a mark or impression
to form is to make or shape

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that the impression they leave is like a bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaped like a tooth, which is what toothy means in this technical sense.

clue.text: He has to look after an obstinate lot.

definitions.text: He has to look after an obstinate lot.

parts.words: He has to look after an obstinate lot
parts.note: sounds like a teacher with an unruly class, but the stubborn charges are mules

explanation.surface: A carer is burdened with a stubborn group of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver of mules tends animals proverbially known for stubbornness.

clue.text: Ices soup, perhaps just making a

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Ices soup, perhaps just making a (8)', is cut short: the anagram of ICES SOUP is plain but the defining words after 'making a' are missing.

clue.text: Useful hint to send about someone's salary.

indicators.note: about means the word send goes around the hint

parts.note: taken as written
a tip is a useful hint

explanation.surface: Advice on forwarding someone's pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed regular allowance or pay, especially for a clergyman.

clue.text: A Spanish nobleman is maybe a

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'A Spanish nobleman is maybe a (6)', is cut short: A + DON + IS is plain but the defining words for a handsome young man are missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: A Spanish nobleman is maybe a

clue.text: No longer impediments to putting directions.

definitions.text: No longer impediments to putting directions.

parts.words: No longer impediments to putting directions
parts.note: in golf, a ball blocking another's line to the hole on the green was once an allowed obstruction, abolished in 1952

explanation.surface: Obstacles to issuing instructions have been removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' means golf putting, not placing. The golfing stymie, where an opponent's ball blocked your putt, was abolished in 1952.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfing obstructions on the green where one ball blocked another's line, a rule since dropped.

clue.text: Lighter type of blue ?

parts.note: Cambridge's sporting colour is a paler blue than Oxford's, and a sportsman awarded it is a blue

explanation.surface: A question about pale shades of colour.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'blue' is a sportsman who has represented Oxford or Cambridge; Cambridge blue is the lighter shade.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cambridge University member, whose sporting blue is the pale shade.

clue.text: It's proof against anything, this, brute villainy.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'It's proof against anything, this, brute villainy.', has no anagram indicator and BRUTE VILLAINY is two letters (I, N) short of the answer, so words are missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: It's proof against anything, this, brute villainy.

clue.text: Utter-but not out-and-out.

parts.note: utter as an adjective means out-and-out, but here it is the verb meaning to say

explanation.surface: A paradox about something complete yet not complete.
explanation.definitionFit: To express something in words, the verbal sense of utter rather than its sense of total.

clue.text: An race to honour lost." (Burns)

parts.note: a line from Burns where the missing word describes a foolish dynasty

explanation.surface: A quotation from Robert Burns about a disgraced line of kings.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns, Lines on Stirling: 'An idiot race, to honour lost'. Fill the gap after 'An'.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns calls the later Stuarts a foolish, witless race; the gap takes the word for a fool.

clue.text: Fancy a mere abridgement ending big volume!

definitions.text: Fancy a mere abridgement ending big volume!

parts.words: Fancy a mere abridgement ending big volume
parts.note: a short summary whose final letters spell a word for a large book, which is the joke

explanation.surface: Surprise that a short digest should finish as a weighty book.
explanation.walkthrough: A summary is an abridgement, yet the word itself ends in TOME, a big volume.
explanation.definitionFit: A summary or condensed account, an abridgement of a larger work.

clue.text: . Sort of oil found on a jaunt in Africa.

indicators.note: found on places the rearranged oil after the jaunt in this across entry

parts.note: a trip is a jaunt

indicators.note: sort of means the letters of oil are put into another order

explanation.surface: Oil discovered during an excursion across Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading full stop is a scanning stray. TRIPOLI is the capital of Libya.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the capital city of Libya on the North African coast.

clue.text: Visionary type one might say.

parts.note: an idealist with fanciful notions, described loosely

explanation.surface: A loose description of an idealist.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealist who imagines impractical schemes, the kind of person called a visionary.

clue.text: Somewhat early to see Timothy busy ones?

indicators.note: to see suggests the name appears within the busy insects

parts.note: bees are proverbially busy

explanation.surface: An early start to visit Timothy and his busy colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to see' is a loose container signal: the name is seen within the insects. BETIMES is an old word, still met in literature.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for early or in good time.
